title: VPC control-plane playbook for security architects
body:
Purpose and audience:
This is a concise, technical playbook for security architects, SRE leads, and procurement reviewers who are evaluating Redwood’s Private (VPC / on-prem) control-plane option. The goal: give security teams the exact language, threat model, telemetry commitments, and negotiable contract levers they expect — in one place — so solutions engineering and sales can move faster with fewer rounds of legal/security review.

How this doc should be used:
- Primary users: security architects, platform engineering reviewers, procurement technical evaluators.
- Secondary users: solutions engineering and account execs prepping an RFP response or demo.
- Tone: technical, factual, and pragmatic. Assume the reader understands cloud networking and compliance frameworks.

Top-level positioning to lead with (30s elevator):
"Redwood Private separates control-plane metadata from customer data: control-plane orchestration and telemetry can be hosted or self-managed, while inference workloads and all request/response data remain in your VPC or on-prem. We provide tight scoping of telemetry, optional air-gapped deployments, and contract-level commitments for retention, deletion, and key custody."

Common security questions and model answers (short):
- Where does model inference data flow?
  - Answer: In all Private modes inference requests and responses are routed to compute inside the customer's VPC or on-prem nodes. The control plane only sees resource identifiers, configuration hashes, and non-PII usage metrics unless explicitly enabled.
- Do you persist prompts/responses outside my network?
  - Answer: By default, no. Telemetry is optional and off for regulated deployments; if enabled, data is hashed/aggregated in-flight and retained per contract. We offer a zero-retention telemetry mode.
- Can Redwood access customer keys or models?
  - Answer: No. Key material for model encryption and VM images is customer-managed via KMS/HSM integrations. We provide operational runbooks to rotate keys and verify image signatures.
- How do you handle security incidents and forensics?
  - Answer: We provide a runbook with a primary contact, expected timelines, and a forensic artifact checklist. For Private deployments we can run investigations inside the customer environment; artifacts can be exported to customer SIEMs.

Control-plane semantics — precise language to use:
- "Control plane": orchestration, resource tracking, model registry pointers, configuration and rollout policies. It does NOT include any request/response payloads unless telemetry is explicitly turned on.
- "Data plane": inference compute inside customer VPC or on-prem hosts — this is where tokens/payloads traverse.
- "Telemetry": aggregated metrics, anonymized latency/cost stats, and optional prompt hashing for quality monitoring (disabled by default).
- "Hosted control plane": Redwood-managed service that stores metadata and routes jobs. Offerings: standard telemetry (aggregated), limited telemetry (hash-only), or zero-telemetry (contracted).
- "Customer-controlled control plane": customer-hosted instance of the control plane components (air-gapped or VPC) with full auditability.

Threat model & mitigation summary (for security reviewers):
- Risk: Lateral movement from control plane to data plane.
  - Mitigation: No control-plane access to customer VMs; authenticated job tokens are scoped and rotated; network-level ACLs and private peering; optional host-based firewall rules.
- Risk: Sensitive data leakage via telemetry.
  - Mitigation: Telemetry off by default for regulated deployments; when enabled, telemetry is hashed and aggregated; retention periods contractually limited; auditing of telemetry access.
- Risk: Supply-chain compromise (build/image tampering).
  - Mitigation: Signed builds, reproducible build artifacts, image provenance logs; optional customer-side image signing requirement.
- Risk: Insider access to model registry and configuration.
  - Mitigation: RBAC, MFA, audit logs shipped to customer SIEM, and support for SCIM provisioning to enforce corporate SSO policies.

Negotiable contractual levers (what security teams often ask for):
- Telemetry retention: zero/30/90/365 days.
- Telemetry scope: full / aggregated-only / hash-only / none.
- Audit log exports: push to customer S3/GCS/OCI or Syslog endpoint.
- Data processing addendum: explicit language forbidding Redwood from training or improving models on customer data and required attestations.
- On-call access: define whether Redwood engineers can SSH/jump into control-plane hosts; prefer ticketed ephemeral access into customer-hosted control plane.
- Subpoena/legal support: reciprocal notice timelines and redaction commitments where allowed.

Operational checklist (pre-eval items customers will ask for):
- Network: required CIDR ranges for peering, egress rules, and TLS cert thumbprints.
- IAM: least-privilege roles, SCIM group mappings, and recommended role names.
- KMS: supported providers (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, Google KMS, HashiCorp Vault) and sample key policy.
- Images: recommended base images, signing process, and checksum verification steps.
- Monitoring: minimal metric set we need for capacity vs. optional telemetry set for model quality.

Sample objection scripts and rebuttals (sales + SE friendly):
- Objection: "We can't allow any external control plane touching our environment."
  - Script: "Totally reasonable. We offer a customer-controlled control plane where all orchestration components run in your VPC or an air-gapped cluster. Redwood provides deployment artifacts and an optional managed-support contract for runbook-driven incidents."
- Objection: "Your telemetry looks invasive."
  - Script: "Telemetry is off by default for regulated customers. If you enable it we can restrict to hashed, aggregated metrics and write a retention clause into the contract. We can also push telemetry outputs to your own storage."
- Objection: "What if you need to debug an incident?"
  - Script: "We use a ticketed support flow; debug sessions are live and recorded, require customer approval, and can be executed entirely inside your environment in customer-hosted control plane mode. For critical incidents we share forensics artifacts per the agreed SLA."

Competitive notes (how to differentiate succinctly):
- Public cloud vendor endpoints: often simpler but conflate control+data plane and keep more telemetry; Redwood differentiates by strict separation and contractable telemetry.
- Pure self-hosted inference vendors: may require full ops team to maintain orchestration; Redwood offers a hybrid pattern (customer control plane with optional managed support) to lower ops burden.
- Other LLM API providers: typically don't offer customer-hosted control plane or KMS integrations; emphasize our KMS/HSM support and audit export capabilities.

Redlines & hard no's for legal/security (what we rarely concede):
- Redwood will not accept unlimited telemetry retention requests without additional commercial terms.
- We do not assume ownership of customer model IP; customers keep model assets and keys.
- We will not submit to export-controlled code installation that breaks local laws; require lawful request process.

Next steps & templates to attach (work-in-progress list):
- Ship a short "control-plane promise" one-pager for security reviews (TBD).
- Add a sample KMS key policy and SCIM mapping example to the repo (PR 87 is the starter).
- Create a short demo script for customer-hosted control-plane installation (internal runbook).

Notes to solutions engineering:
- When prepping docs, ask the buyer if telemetry will be allowed and what retention they require — this determines whether to propose hosted vs customer-hosted control plane.
- Keep the conversation concrete: bring CIDR ranges, expected throughput, and sample audit log format (we have templates in the repo).
- If legal asks for data-training clauses, use the standard DPA + data processing addendum draft and escalate to the security PM for any deviations.

Unresolved questions (for product/security to decide):
- Do we offer a standardized zero-telemetry SLA for all enterprise contracts or only by exception?
- What is the minimum set of hashed telemetry needed for automated rollout safety checks?

End of playbook — quick reference checklist for meetings:
1) Ask: "Will telemetry be allowed? If yes, what retention?"
2) Clarify deployment mode: hosted-control-plane, customer-hosted control-plane (VPC), or air-gapped on-prem.
3) Share: key artifacts — KMS policy, SCIM mappings, audit log sample.
4) Confirm: where forensic artifacts should be exported (customer SIEM / S3 / GCS).

Footnote: This document is intentionally operational and slightly informal. Add real examples / log samples once legal signs off on the telemetry retention templates.
